items.title: 26.3 Identifying the Type, Repeat Unit and Monomers of a Polymer

source_refs.note: Topic 26.3 with Table 26.1 and the first Quick Check 26.2, answered (PDF 152-154); the examples are redrawn. The condensation example is captioned '(addition)' in the book. Answer (i) depends on reading the printed section. Answers need review.

blocks.text: To identify a polymer from a skeletal or structural formula, look for the repeating linkage and the monomer units. Only addition and condensation polymers are considered here.

items: Identify the type: look at the main chain (backbone). If it contains only carbon atoms (-C-C-C-), it is an addition polymer, formed from alkenes. If it contains oxygen or nitrogen as well as carbon, it is a condensation polymer. A C=O next to O shows an ester link (polyester, e.g. PET); a C=O next to N-H shows an amide (peptide) link (polyamide, e.g. nylon-6,6 or Kevlar).
Find the repeat unit: look for where the sequence starts to repeat, place brackets round one repeating section and add the subscript n.

Find the monomer(s): for an addition polymer, change the C-C single bond of the repeat unit back into C=C. For a condensation polymer, add water back: break the ester or amide bond, adding -OH to the C=O side and -H to the O or N side.
